articles.title: Security incident at U.S.-run air base almost certainly directed by Iran, U.K. prime minister says
articles.summary: The U.S. pulled its bombers last week from RAF Fairford, and the Pentagon said all American bombers at the facility had been redeployed to their home bases.
articles.body: LONDON — A suspected terrorist plot at a U.S.-run military air base in England was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday. Burnham previously said there are strong indications Iran was linked to the apparent plan last month to attack the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran in the ongoing war. Police have arrested seven men in the investigation into the alleged plot, but all suspects have been released on bail and no one has been charged so far. Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” Burnham told lawmakers. “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil.” Scores of residents near the air base were evacuated from their homes on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the initial five suspects who were arrested on the scene, but no explosives. All the suspects arrested are in their 20s. Six are British nationals while one is a dual U.K.-Iranian citizen. The U.S. pulled its bombers last week from RAF Fairford, about 100 miles west of London, and the Pentagon said all American bombers at the facility had been redeployed to their home bases in the U.S. The Trump administration has said it believed the base faced Iranian threats intended to kill as many American troops and destroy as many U.S. planes as possible. The British government allowed the U.S. military to use RAF Fairford for what it called defensive strikes on Iranian missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on U.K. interests and Britain’s allies in the Gulf. On Monday, the British government summoned the Iranian ambassador to express displeasure at “Iran’s continued attempts to undermine the security of the United Kingdom and international partners through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity.” It also said it added two Iranians, including the head of counterespionage operations in the Revolutionary Guard, to its sanctioned list. Iran and allied militant groups have previously been accused of plotting or carrying out attacks on U.S., British and Jewish targets, allegedly acting through local proxies. In a joint statement released Monday, the foreign ministers of more than two dozen Western countries condemned Iranian attacks on their territories through proxies or other means. “Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts,” the statement said.

articles.title: Ethiopian forces enter strategic Tigray town of Adwa, witnesses say
articles.summary: Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights to Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, on Sunday.
articles.body:
Ethiopian government forces have entered the town of Adwa without a fight, days after capturing Adigrat from rebel fighters as flights resumed to Mekelle in the country’s northern Tigray region.

Residents of the northwestern town of Adwa, roughly 40km (24 miles) from Eritrea’s border, said federal forces and an allied militia entered the town on Sunday, a day after the withdrawal of fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).

TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa said he “did not wish to comment”.

“All the shops in the town are closed. Last night, many government institutions, including Adwa Hospital, were looted,” Aferwerki, a local resident who gave only one name, told AFP.

Conflict monitor ACLED said that Ethiopian drone strikes targeted a hotel in Adwa on October 4, wounding between “five and nine people, including security personnel”, who were taken to hospital. Some ACLED sources indicated that TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael and other senior officials were at the hotel, but stressed the information had not been verified.

Another resident who requested anonymity confirmed the TPLF forces withdrew from Adwa but said that although government forces were deployed in the town, they had not reached the centre.

“The roads are deserted. People are very afraid of theft,” he said.

Last week, Ethiopian forces captured Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle, days after the TPLF confirmed that it had withdrawn from the city and moved its regional administration “temporarily” to another location.

Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights from the capital, Addis Abba, to Mekelle on Sunday for the first time since September 23, when a seven-group armed alliance , including the TPLF, started fighting Ethiopian forces and captured the airport.

“I would like to assure you on this occasion that we will bring visible change, a change beyond mere hope,” Getachew Reda, a former Tigray leader who now advises Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed told supporters greeting Reda and Ethiopia’s intelligence chief Redwan Hussein at Mekelle airport.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the rebel alliance.

Khartoum and Cairo have denied involvement. Eritrea, which fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army in the 2020-2022 war, severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia over the accusations last week.

articles.title: Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France following arrests
articles.summary: Renoir art heist suspects were planning ‘imminent’ second robbery, prosecutors say.
articles.body:
Two paintings by the impressionist master Renoir which were stolen from a French museum last month have been found damaged behind a false wall in a private home after police made several arrests ahead of what prosecutors say was an imminent second heist.

Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said six suspects were arrested on Wednesday after authorities discovered they were planning to target the Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, home to one of Europe’s largest collections of modern art.

Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent”.

“We were very clearly looking at the repetition of a criminal scheme”, said Eric Antonetti, the head of the Alpes-Maritimes judicial police.

On September 8, thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence to enter the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera, according to investigators.

An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that “apparently caused the perpetrators to panic,” Bessone said.

The stolen works, “Madame Colonna Romano” and “Young Woman at the Well” by impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, were valued at about 4.2m euros ($4.7m), Bessone said.

The thieves also attempted to steal two other Renoir paintings, “Madame Pichon” and “Coco Reading”, which depicts Renoir’s young ‌son ‌Claude. They abandoned them in the museum gardens while fleeing police.

“As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve,” he said.

The paintings were found hidden behind a false wall in a house on Friday. Both works were damaged and will need ⁠restoration. One of the paintings, “Madame Colonna Romano”, had been torn.

“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, said on Friday. “Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”

The recovery came almost exactly one month ⁠after the theft, following an investigation that used ⁠DNA evidence, mobile phone geolocation data and surveillance video.

The two key suspects include a 29-year-old, who was charged after investigators recovered DNA from a bag left behind during the getaway.

They ⁠were charged with organised theft and other offences. A third man, accused of hiding the paintings, was charged with organised handling of stolen goods.

A fourth suspect, who investigators say was approached about buying the artworks, was charged ‌with handling stolen goods and taking part in a criminal conspiracy.

Bessone said the suspects had denied planning a second museum raid, but he added that he did “not believe the principal suspect visited that ‌museum simply out of a love of art”.

articles.title: British adventurer returns home after 28-year walk around the world
articles.summary: Adventurer Karl Bushby swam the English Channel and celebrated with fish and chips after his 28-year, 30,000-mile walk from Chile to England.
articles.body: Adventurer Karl Bushby has finally stepped foot on UK soil after a 28-year journey across the world. On Oct. 5, he announced he swam the English Channel, from France to England. While resting in Dover, he said, "I’m staring at the Union Jack flying outside this hotel. I’ve seen many flags over the days, but that one is special." On social media he shared one of his first meals back, overjoyed to have authentic British fish and chips again. DALE 'GREY BEARD' SANDERS RECLAIMS TITLE AS OLDEST PERSON TO THRU-HIKE THE APPALACHIAN TRAIL AT 91 His journey is not over yet. He hopes to reach the finish line — his mother’s home in Hull — by the end of the month. According to his website, he received a birthday card in the 1990s from his father about two soldiers arguing over an impossible feat, walking from London to New York via the Bering Strait. Karl grabbed a map and drew a single line, knowing he found his life’s mission. NAVY VETERANS REUNITE AFTER 30 YEARS FOR 'GRUELING' CROSS-COUNTRY BIKE CHALLENGE HONORING 9/11 On Nov. 1, 1998, the ex-paratrooper started his journey in Chile, with only a few hundred dollars in his pocket "South America, you were young, it was all new, it was the boys adventure dream," Bushby said. He walked north to the United States, waiting for the Bering Strait to freeze to cross from Alaska into Russia. In April 2012, Russia denied his next visa, pausing his expedition. So he started walking in the wrong direction, in protest, to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C. The ban was overturned and he carried on with his journey. From Russia he entered Mongolia, China, and swam the Caspian Sea from Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan. Then it was on to Europe. "You’ll find that you are way more capable than you think you are, people always underestimate themselves. The world always looks bigger and scarier than it actually is," Bushby said. MAN WHO BEAT RARE CANCER CELEBRATES BY CANOEING 2,000 MILES WITH HIS DOG He originally expected the journey to take 12 years, but visa restrictions, the 2008 financial crash, COVID-19, geopolitics, detention and some close calls slowed his progress. He says it’s the people that kept him going. "The world is an incredible place, and it’s the people, the strangers that I have met along the way, that have kept me upright and moving forward," Bushby said. "We went at a reasonable pace, we did what we needed to do and it has worked. I know it’s time to stop, I know that much because I feel that in the knees and ankles."

articles.title: Mamdani calls ICE a 'rogue' agency after NYC shooting, claims agents view law as 'merely a suggestion'
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused ICE of being a "rogue federal agency" after an immigration officer fired seven shots at a man in Manhattan.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) of operating as a "rogue federal agency" and treating the law as "merely a suggestion" during a Sunday interview, days after a federal immigration officer fired seven shots at a man in Manhattan while his 5-year-old son was inside the vehicle. Mamdani, speaking to MS NOW host Jacob Soboroff in his first interview since Thursday's shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, accused ICE agents of repeatedly disregarding the law and questioned whether New Yorkers could distinguish federal officers from dangerous attackers. "We follow the law in New York City and I know that to the secretary, the law is merely a suggestion when it comes to the actions of these ICE agents," Mamdani said. "They are making a mockery of what law and order is." MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS The Department of Homeland Security pushed back against Mamdani's accusations in a statement to Fox News Digital, defending ICE and criticizing the mayor's rhetoric toward federal immigration officers. "ICE enforces the law as written. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S. — full stop," a DHS spokesperson said. "Mayor Mamdani should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from his city — NOT vilifying law enforcement." "Attacks and demonization of ICE law enforcement is wrong," the statement continued. "Because of smears like this our ICE officers are now facing a 1,600% increase in assaults against them as they put their lives on the line to arrest murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists." EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET Mamdani argued that ICE's operations were making New Yorkers less safe and calling for the agency's elimination. "What we see from their actions is an agency that terrorizes, one that creates a sense of fear as opposed to any idea of safety. And I made it very clear that the longer that ICE agents were engaging in their operations in the city, the less safe this city was becoming," Mamdani said. The shooting occurred Thursday afternoon in the Marble Hill neighborhood, where ICE agents attempted to apprehend Belgal, a Dominican national whom DHS said had a prior grand larceny conviction and previous arrests involving assault, robbery, drugs and weapons. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at least one federal immigration officer fired seven rounds, striking Belgal in the neck below his left ear. His 5-year-old son, who was sitting inside the vehicle, was unharmed. Mamdani said he spoke with President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin for nearly two hours Thursday evening in an unsuccessful effort to secure Belgal's release. He expressed frustration with the secretary's assessment of the shooting. "What struck me is the secretary did not think that ICE agents had done anything wrong," Mamdani said. "I am demanding that ICE cease their operations in our city immediately, because these operations make New Yorkers less safe. They leave New Yorkers in a state of terror." DHS SECRETARY BASHES NEW YORK LEADERSHIP AFTER ANNOUNCING THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS IN SWEEPING OPERATION On Friday, U.S. District Judge Paul Oetken temporarily blocked Belgal's deportation while his challenge to federal detention remains pending. The judge also restricted his transfer outside specified federal judicial districts without prior court approval. The NYPD, which was not involved in the shooting, released body camera footage showing officers responding to the scene after the shooting. The FBI and Homeland Security Investigations are investigating the incident. Mullin criticized Mamdani's anti-ICE rhetoric during a Friday news conference, accusing the mayor of inciting hostility toward federal immigration officers while refusing to support their enforcement efforts. "His words are dangerous and incite hostility. It doesn't help," Mullin said. "He said that ICE is rotten to the core. Really? Men and women at ICE each day are enforcing the laws that he refuses to enforce. He said he wants to abolish ICE. Well, Mayor, if you abolish ICE, who's going to take the criminals off the streets of your own town?" The department said the Trump administration's immigration crackdown had resulted in more than 3 million illegal immigrants leaving the United States, including an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations.

articles.title: A Lincolnshire woman kept a box marked ‘broken porcelain’ in her attic for more than 20 years and repeatedly wondered what to do with it; the inherited Chinese pieces were finally taken to auction and sold for more than £160,000
articles.summary: A Lincolnshire woman discovered valuable Chinese porcelain in her attic after over 20 years. The pieces, inherited from her grandfather, sold for £196,992 at auction, far exceeding expectations. Learn more about this remarkable find and the history behind the ceramics.
articles.body: A Lincolnshire woman has sold a collection of inherited Chinese porcelain for more than £160,000 after keeping a box labelled “broken porcelain” in her attic for more than 20 years. The pieces fetched £196,992, including fees, at auction.Gill Stewart rediscovered the box while looking for Christmas decorations at her home in Benniworth, near Louth. She had repeatedly wondered what to do with the items but did not take them to an auctioneer until earlier this year.“I brought it up to Lincolnshire [in 2002] and since then it's just lived in the attic,” Stewart told the BBC. “Every time I went up to get the Christmas decorations, I thought 'I must do something with that box'.”Stewart eventually took the collection to John Taylors Auction Rooms in Louth to find out whether it was worth selling. The auction house divided the pieces into separate lots, which attracted far higher bids than expected.Grandfather's notes helped identify the piecesStewart inherited the porcelain after the death of her grandfather, Brigadier Robert Kellie, who had collected the items while stationed in China around the turn of the 20th century. Some pieces had been damaged over the years, leading to the box being labelled “broken porcelain”.Kellie had kept detailed notes about the collection, including the reign marks, designs and damage to individual pieces. Reign marks record the Chinese dynasty and the emperor's reign during which an object was made.The notes also recorded who had broken some of the items. Stewart told the BBC that her grandfather's records showed her grandmother was responsible for damaging several pieces, including some of the most valuable ones.Auctioneer James Laverack, from John Taylors Auction Rooms, said the collection's appearance did not initially suggest its eventual value.“It's the sort of stuff you would hear about people finding in charity shops or carboots. Most people wouldn't think they're worth more than a pound or two, but they're rare, highly collectable and therefore highly valuable.”Laverack said the auction house sought advice on the pieces because Chinese porcelain can be difficult to assess. Although the team expected interest, it did not anticipate the final result.Porcelain lot estimated at £50 sells for £59,000One of the strongest results came from a lot containing 16 porcelain pieces, including four “month cups” of the type produced at imperial kilns during the Kangxi period, which ran from 1662 to 1722.The lot had been estimated at £50 to £100 but sold for £59,000. The two highest-selling lots went to a UK dealer who was present at the auction, according to The Guardian.Another lot demonstrated how damage did not necessarily prevent the pieces from attracting bidders. One item had been broken and glued back together. An expert told the auction house it could be worth £20,000 in good condition, but its damaged state led to an estimate of just £100. It ultimately sold for £5,000.Laverack said interest in the collection became increasingly clear as the auction approached, although the team remained uncertain about the outcome until the sale.He called Stewart after her lots had finished selling to tell her the result. Stewart had not watched the auction and was taken aback when she heard the figure.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Texas hiker found dead after going missing in Great Smoky Mountains, family says
articles.summary: Sahil Jilani's phone, keys, and clothes were found near Abrams Falls before dive teams recovered his body in Tennessee's Great Smoky Mountains.
articles.body: A Texas hiker has been found dead three days after going missing in Tennessee's Great Smoky Mountains, with his family believing he drowned after becoming caught in powerful hydraulic currents near a waterfall. Sahil Jilani, a 24-year-old resident of Houston, died after disappearing on Oct. 5 — the same day that left his mother with an "overwhelming feeling that something was terribly wrong." His family announced the tragedy through an online fundraiser. "It is with heavy hearts and profound sorrow that we share the sudden, heartbreaking loss of our beloved brother, Sahil Jilani, and the hospitalization of our mother after learning she had lost her precious son, our little angel and most beautiful gift," the fundraiser stated. BODY OF MISSING HIKER FOUND IN OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK THANKS TO CRUCIAL CLUE Loved ones grew concerned when Jilani failed to check in for several hours and his location-sharing stopped in an area with no cell service. "We were advised to be patient, as hikers and campers frequently lose contact in areas without network coverage," wrote Jilani's sister Asma Jilani Bustamante who organized the fundraiser. "But as the hours passed, our fear grew, and we continued requesting help. Sahil knew how much his silence and unavailable location would worry us." NPS INVESTIGATES AFTER 23-YEAR-OLD REPORTEDLY SWEPT OVER NOTORIOUS YOSEMITE WATERFALL After he had been missing for 72 hours, Jilani's car was discovered in a parking lot, with his phone, keys and clothes later recovered near the falls. The following day, dive teams pulled his body from the waters at Abrams Falls. Family members believe Jilani drowned after becoming trapped in powerful water currents. TOURISTS CLING TO EACH OTHER IN DESPERATE STRUGGLE AS RAGING FLOOD SWEEPS THEM DOWN WATERFALL "Waterfalls are breathtakingly beautiful, and many visitors naturally want to stand beneath them and feel the pressure of the falling water," the family said. "What many don't realize is that Abrams Falls drops approximately 25 feet into a deep pool of water where hydraulic currents can pull a person underwater and trap them in recirculating water, making escape extremely difficult, even for experienced swimmers." An official cause of death has not yet been disclosed. MULTIPLE HIKERS DEAD AMID SCORCHING GRAND CANYON TEMPERATURES Jilani had recently become an uncle and was "beyond excited to spoil his little niece with gifts and teach her mixed martial arts and self-defense, sharing his passion for fitness," Bustamante said. National Park Service (NPS) officials warn that the Smoky Mountains contain narrow roads, blind curves, and steep drop-offs. Additionally, the park does not feature any lifeguarded swimming areas. The rocks are coated with slippery algae, and several hikers have fallen and been seriously injured or killed." Fox News Digital has reached out to the National Park Service for further comment.

articles.title: Teen girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual plummet in stunning reversal, new data shows
articles.summary: Teen girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual dropped from 30% to 17% in four years, according to CDC data highlighted by The Washington Post.
articles.body: The number of teenage girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual has plunged in just four years, according to new data highlighted by The Washington Post, revealing a dramatic shift in how young Americans describe their sexual orientation and leaving researchers searching for answers. The share of ninth-grade girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual dropped from 30% in 2021 to just 17% in 2025, while those identifying as bisexual alone fell by half, from 26% to 13%, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data cited in the report. The percentage of boys identifying as gay or bisexual has remained largely unchanged over the past decade, while the share of high school girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual surged following the COVID-19 pandemic before beginning to decline, the Post reported. GALLUP POLL FINDS AMERICANS' SUPPORT FOR LGBTQ+ ISSUES SLIDING BACKWARD AMID CULTURAL SHIFT Although those numbers have continued to fall, rates among older teenage girls have remained relatively steady and are still higher than before the pandemic, the outlet reported. Jean Twenge, a professor of psychology at San Diego State University who published her analysis of the 2025 data on her Substack "Generation Tech," told The Washington Post that the downward trend began while former President Joe Biden was still in office, casting doubt on whether the shift could be attributed to a change in presidential administrations. In a recent post on X about the development, Terry Schilling, president of the American Principles Project wrote, "Amazing what happens when you cut the Department of Education and USAID." The available data also does not explain why such a political transition would affect certain age groups differently, according to The Washington Post. DETRANSITIONER CHLOE COLE CANCELS UW SPEECH AFTER ALLEGED ANTIFA THREATS Walt Heyer, who detransitioned 40 years ago after identifying as a woman for eight years and author of many books, including "Trans Life Survivors," cautioned against drawing sweeping conclusions from the findings, telling Fox News Digital that more research is needed before declaring a lasting shift. "Better to be skeptical and conduct more studies before we put this study in the win column."

articles.title: Julia Child and her husband built La Pitchoune in Provence in 1963 and used it for nearly three decades; after she gave it up in 1992, the home became a cooking school where guests still cook in her original kitchen
articles.summary: Julia Child and her husband, Paul, built La Pitchoune in Provence in 1963 as a place to cook, entertain and return to year after year.
articles.body: Julia Child and her husband, Paul, built La Pitchoune in Provence in 1963 as a place to cook, entertain and return to year after year. The small stucco house became their summer retreat for nearly three decades, its kitchen shaped around Julia’s personality and practical approach to cooking. When she gave up the property in 1992, it did not become just another quiet country home. It went on to serve as a cooking school, and today visitors can still prepare meals in the kitchen where Child worked. Colorado’s Coloradan and Eater have both told the story of the house’s later life, describing how its owners have preserved the original kitchen while welcoming cooks to experience the space for themselves. Read on to know more details about it here:A little house in ProvenceLa Pitchoune, which means “the little one,” sits near the village of Plascassier in the hills above Cannes. The Childs built it on land owned by Julia’s close friend and cookbook collaborator Simone Beck and her husband, Jean Fischbacher. It was modest compared with the grand villas often associated with the French Riviera, but its setting and kitchen made it a special place for the couple.For nearly 30 years, Julia and Paul returned to the house, spending time there cooking and entertaining. The home became part of their rhythm of life in Provence, a place where Julia could work with the ingredients and techniques that had helped make French cooking approachable to American readers. The kitchen was designed around the way Julia cooked. Its counters were unusually high, a practical choice for someone who stood more than six feet tall. Paul installed pegboards on the walls so pots and utensils could hang within easy reach. He traced the outline of each tool on the boards, making it simple to see where everything belonged, as per the reports.The kitchen that stayedWhen Julia and Paul gave up the house in 1992, Paul’s health was declining. The property passed back to the Beck family, and its story took a new direction. A former student of Beck’s later owned La Pitchoune and ran a cooking school there, continuing its association with food and learning.The kitchen, however, remained the home’s most meaningful feature. Coloradan reported that its tall counters and pegboards were still in place when the Held family took over the property. The outlines of the original utensils remained visible, preserving a small but vivid record of how Julia organised her workspace. The kitchen matters not only because it belonged to a famous chef, but because it was built for use. The cookware, knives, baking dishes and work surfaces invite guests to prepare food rather than simply look around. Visitors can experience the room as a working kitchen, where practical details reveal how Julia approached cooking.A family takes on the legacyCraig Held and his family acquired La Pitchoune in 2016, after his daughter Makenna became concerned that someone might renovate the house beyond recognition. She had read about the property and felt strongly that its kitchen should be preserved. Makenna had trained at Le Cordon Bleu and wanted to protect the space while sharing it with other people who loved food. The Held family began operating La Pitchoune as both a vacation rental and a cooking school. Their aim was to preserve the house without turning it into a museum visitors could only observe from a distance, as per the reports.The family welcomes guests with food and wine and provides access to the kitchen, including the pots, pans, knives and baking dishes needed to cook. Coloradan reported that the property could be rented for stays of up to six adults, while the Courageous Cooking School offered live-in classes and excursions led by Makenna.That combination gives visitors a chance to experience the home at a slower pace. They can shop for ingredients, cook together and spend time in the same kitchen where Julia’s culinary life in Provence unfolded.Cooking where Julia cookedThe appeal of La Pitchoune rests partly in its authenticity. There are replicas of Julia Child’s kitchen in museums, but the house in Provence preserves the original room in its original setting. Its tall counters, familiar pegboards and surrounding landscape create a sense of continuity that a display case cannot reproduce.Food writer Julia Moskin described staying and cooking there in a 2016 New York Times feature, writing that the kitchen felt largely unchanged. The experience of using the space is central to the house’s identity. Guests are not merely touring Julia’s former home; they are preparing meals in it.The cooking school builds on that idea with practical instruction. Participants can learn techniques, work with local ingredients and take part in excursions around the region. Rather than treating Julia’s legacy as something fixed in the past, the school keeps it active through the everyday work of cooking.A legacy made to be usedLa Pitchoune has outlasted its original purpose as a private summer retreat. It became a cooking school after Julia gave it up, then evolved into a place where visitors can rent the house and learn in its kitchen. Each new chapter has kept the property connected to food.That continuity feels fitting for a chef whose influence came from making cooking accessible. Julia Child’s work encouraged people to try unfamiliar recipes, learn through practice and enjoy the process of preparing a meal. At La Pitchoune, guests can follow that spirit in the very room where she once cooked.The house has not been frozen in time, but its most important details remain. The pegboards still show where utensils belonged, and the high counters still reflect the needs of their original owner. More than three decades after Julia left, the kitchen continues to welcome people to cook, eat and learn.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Chicago police find killer in 65-year-old cold case murder of little girl — one of their own
articles.summary: DNA technology that didn’t exist when Gloria Kowalewicz, 8, was killed in 1960 led investigators to Thomas F. McInerney Jr., who was a homicide detective for the Chicago Police Department.
articles.body: The cold case murder of an 8-year-old Chicago girl that bedeviled investigators for 65 years has been solved — and the man tied to the killing was a homicide detective for the city’s police department. The murder of Gloria Kowalewicz, who was abducted Nov. 12, 1960, as she was walking to church on the South Side of Chicago, sparked a citywide manhunt that went on for months, during which thousands of people were questioned and hundreds of leads were looked into. But it wasn’t until July that a DNA technology that didn’t exist when Gloria was killed, combined with “a carefully preserved fingerprint,” led investigators to Thomas F. McInerney Jr., the Chicago Police Department said in a statement to NBC News. It was the same technology that was used to capture Joseph James DeAngelo, a former California cop dubbed “The Golden State Killer,” who committed 13 murders and numerous rapes from the mid-1970s to the mid-1980s and is serving life in prison. But unlike DeAngelo, McInerney managed to escape justice. McInerney retired from the Chicago Police Department in 1987 as a detective after 28 years on the job and died in 2006 at age 70 in Las Vegas. “McInerney should never have worn the CPD star, and it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive,” the CPD said in a statement Monday. Gloria’s brother, Adam Kowalewicz — who was an infant when his sister was killed — agreed. “The one thing that does play in my mind [is], unfortunately, he lived a decent life and passed on,” Kowalewicz said of McInerney in an interview with the Chicago Tribune. “He never paid his dues. You hope he’s going to pay his dues with the good lord.” Then there is the nagging question that, so far, police haven’t been able to answer: Why did McInerney target Gloria? McInerney’s parents lived less than a mile from the Kowalewicz family, but McInerney doesn’t appear to have had any previous contact with the little girl, police said. That having been said, McInerney’s DNA is in the FBI’s Combined DNA Index System, known as CODIS, and the agency is checking whether there might be any other victims. “Based on the evidence in the Kowalewicz case, and law enforcement’s profiling of child predators and their victimology, we are pursuing every investigative lead that may bring closure on other potential unsolved crimes that occurred during that time period in our area,” the FBI said in a statement. On the last day of her life, a Saturday, Gloria left home just before 8 a.m. to walk to morning Mass a few blocks away at St. Mary of Mount Carmel Church, police said. Gloria, a third grader who just recently had her First Communion, was dressed in a pink-and-brown checkered dress and a blue leotard that her mother had picked out for her, the Tribune reported. “She never made it to mass,” the police said in a statement. “Somewhere between her home and the church that Saturday morning, Gloria was abducted.” Gloria was fatally shot twice in the head and left in a ditch in a forest preserve southwest of Chicago, police said. Her body was found by a motorist who spotted Gloria’s colorful dress and went to investigate. “Evidence was collected and carefully inventoried and preserved — a bullet, Gloria’s coat, her shoes, her white communion purse containing her prayer book,” police said. “Investigators also lifted a fingerprint from the strap of Gloria’s purse.” But police couldn’t pin the crime on anyone. Four days after Gloria was killed, more than 1,000 people attended her funeral at St. Mary of Mount Carmel Church. McInerney, at the time, was a 24-year-old patrol officer based on Chicago’s west side and wasn’t promoted to detective until 1964. It wasn’t immediately clear whether McInerney was ever involved in Gloria’s murder investigation. After he left the CPD and moved to Nevada, he worked for the Federal Public Defender’s Office as an investigator. McInerney retired from that job in 2004, according to his obituary in the Tribune. He was even named Outstanding Federal Defender Investigator in 2003. McInerney, an Army veteran, was also a father of five and a grandfather, his obituary noted. Meanwhile, detectives continued to work Gloria’s case as the evidence sat in storage. “Even as the case seemed frozen in time, the Chicago Police Department never forgot the little girl and never stopped searching for her killer,” police said. The first tantalizing break in the case, police said, came in 2010, when investigators were able to build a male DNA profile of the potential killer from traces of semen found on Gloria’s clothes. But that didn’t yield any arrests. Then, in 2024, at the request of Chicago police, the FBI compared the DNA on the clothing with other genetic samples submitted to family tree research websites and identified McInerney from the semen samples. Armed with a name, they matched McInerney’s fingerprints from his 1959 CPD job application to the fingerprint found on Gloria’s purse strap, police said. “Identification was made through a fingerprint and DNA left behind at the crime scene,” the CPD said in a statement.

articles.title: Christian woman pleads not guilty to new 'Orwellian' charges for standing in silent prayer
articles.summary: British Christian Isabel Vaughan-Spruce's attorney argues the UK crossed a red line by prosecuting someone for private thoughts and silent prayer.
articles.body: A British Christian activist facing fresh criminal charges over silent prayer near an abortion clinic is warning that her country is becoming increasingly "Orwellian," telling Fox News Digital that ordinary citizens are growing afraid to pray in public as her legal battle heads toward trial. "It certainly seems very Orwellian and a lot of people have mentioned that particular word to me," Isabel Vaughan-Spruce told Fox News Digital in an interview Monday. "It seems that we're really fostering a sense of intolerance in our communities." Vaughan-Spruce, co-director of March for Life UK, spoke to Fox News Digital after pleading not guilty in January to new charges in Birmingham, England, in a case that her attorneys argue tests the limits of religious freedom and the government's authority to regulate conduct near abortion facilities. FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP DOJ REACHES SETTLEMENT WITH PRO-LIFE PROTESTER TARGETED BY BIDEN ADMIN She previously received a 13,000 British pounds out-of-court settlement from police after pursuing claims of wrongful arrest and false imprisonment stemming from her earlier arrests for silently praying near an abortion clinic. Now, Vaughan-Spruce says she is facing another charge after returning to pray silently near the same facility following the introduction of nationwide abortion clinic buffer zones in October 2024. Vaughan-Spruce told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview that the controversy has fostered intolerance toward people with differing religious and moral beliefs. "I don't believe that those who are pro-life or Christian should be treated as some kind of social pariah," she added. "A lot of people are just worried about what might happen to them as well because of this," Vaughan-Spruce added. "And I've heard that from a lot of people, you know, just concerned simply about something as simple as praying when they're in a public space." BIBLE VERSE LEADS TO TRIAL IN EUROPE. GROWING CRACKDOWN THREATENS OUR US-UK VALUES She said she is concerned about the longstanding implications of what policies like buffer zones will have on free speech. "I think we need to know our rights and to exercise our rights, and not to be intimidated by other people with [sic] this regard, and particularly our rights under God as Christians to be able to pray wherever we want to pray, certainly if it's something internal in our heads, and not to kind of end up self-censoring because of that prayer is a very, very important part of our life of Christian life," Vaughan-Spruce said. "And we certainly need more of that on the streets, prayer, not less." ORTHODOX JEW ASKS SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CASE AFTER CITY ALLEGEDLY TARGETED HIS HOME PRAYER GROUP Her attorney, Jeremiah Igunnubole, described the prosecution as the first of its kind in Britain and argued that the case raises a fundamental question about whether the government can punish someone for thoughts and private prayer rather than outward conduct. "To be clear, standing within the buffer zone is not a crime," Igunnubole told Fox News Digital. "So the question exactly, the precise question is exactly what has Isabel been charged for? We can only say it's been for her thoughts and the fact that she lifted up her heart and mind to God in prayer." ORTHODOX JEW FIGHTS BACK, SAYS CALIFORNIA CITY FINED HIM FOR HOME PRAYER MEETINGS Asked where the line should be drawn when it comes to freedom of speech, Igunnubole argued that the government should never have the power to regulate an individual's private thoughts. "It certainly is not when the state purports to regulate the thoughts of any individual, and we think that that is a red line that cannot be crossed in the UK under the Human Rights Act," Igunnubole said. "There's an absolute right to freedom of thought and that means that there's no qualifications allowed or permitted." Fox News Digital reached out to the Home Office and the Crown Prosecution Service for comment, who declined to comment due to the pending case. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for playing Walter White Jr. on ‘Breaking Bad,’ dies at 34
articles.summary: Actor RJ Mitte, known for playing the son of Walter White in the hit AMC series “Breaking Bad” and as an advocate for the rights of those with disabilities, has died at the age of 34, his representatives said Monday.
articles.body: Actor RJ Mitte, known for playing the son of Walter White in the hit AMC series “Breaking Bad” and as an advocate for the rights of those with disabilities, has died at the age of 34, his representatives said Monday. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his representatives said. They did not provide details about his cause of death. Mitte died Monday in Brownsville, Texas, where he had moved, Brownsville Justice of the Peace Judge Cyndi Hinojosa said. Hinojosa said she declared him dead at 1:32 p.m. but that she could not disclose the cause of death. In the award-winning “Breaking Bad,” Mitte played Walter White Jr., the teenage son of a high school teacher who becomes a methamphetamine producer. That series, which debuted in January 2008 when he was 15, provided his breakout role. Mitte had cerebral palsy, which was reflected on “Breaking Bad,” and was an advocate for the rights of people living with disabilities. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” his representatives said in the statement. “Beyond entertaining friends and family around the world, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s,” they said in the statement. “He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, while using his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities,” they said. The representatives asked for privacy for Mitte’s family and loved ones. Mitte also starred in the 2020 horror film “The Oak Room” and the 2017 sci-fi film “The Recall.” In “Triumph,” which was released in 2021, Mitte stars as a high schooler who fights to become a wrestler despite having cerebral palsy. That film won a Ruderman Family Foundation Seal of Authentic Representation, an award for the portrayal of people with disabilities. Hinojosa, the justice of the peace, said that Mitte “will be very, very much missed” in Brownsville. “He was so gracious to our town” Hinojosa said in a phone interview. Mitte was born in Jackson, Mississippi, and doctors diagnosed cerebral palsy when he was 3 years old, he told VICE in a 2016 interview. He was 12 or 13 years old when he moved to Los Angeles, he said. “I started acting to meet kids my own age,” he said in the VICE interview. In a 2021 interview, Mitte told “Big Issue” that favorable media and critical reception of “Breaking Bad” helped keep the show on the air in its first few years. “It wasn’t the viewers, because we didn’t have the numbers to stay as a network show,” Mitte said. It wasn’t until later seasons, that “we really got the viewership,” he said. The show ran for five seasons, from 2008 to 2013. In that same interview, Mitte credited his family for supporting him when the public perception of people with cerebral palsy was negative. When he was younger, he said, some believed he would never walk or talk properly or have a typical lifr or career. “That was the perception when I was a kid,” Mitte said in the interview. “And my family was like, ‘No. He’s going to go do things.’” Mitte told VICE in 2016 that he considered himself fortunate to be able to make a difference. “I’m lucky that I can be an advocate. I’m lucky that I can do what I do and talk to the people I get to talk to,” he said. “I think we all have an obligation to have an impact for the positive,” he said.

articles.title: 4 new governors named, picks underline BJP focus on elections
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: President Droupadi Murmu on Monday appointed four new governors - Sudha Yadav of Karnataka, Dhal Singh Bisen of Uttarakhand, Dushyant Gautam of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: President Droupadi Murmu on Monday appointed four new governors - Sudha Yadav of Karnataka, Dhal Singh Bisen of Uttarakhand, Dushyant Gautam of Sikkim and Braj Mohan Ram of Odisha.While Yadav, who hails from Haryana, and Bisen, who is from the agriculturist Bhoyar Pawar caste from MP, belong to the OBC category, both Gautam (Jatav) and Ram (Dhobi) are from SC community, underlining BJP's focus on two demographics which are crucial voting segments in many states, including in poll-bound Uttar Pradesh.Yadav, also a member of BJP parliamentary board, entered politics after her husband, BSF deputy commandant Sukhbir Yadav, was killed in the 1999 Kargil War.The other three appointees are former BJP MPs.The preference for Dalits and OBCs is in line with party's push since 2014 to consolidate the support it has gained among communities which were not part of its core base until PM Narendra Modi's emergence as its mascot. The choices come before assembly elections in party's strongholds of UP and Uttarakhand. Early on, party had fielded a diverse slate of candidates for Rajya Sabha polls from UP, with the coveted berths going to, apart from upper castes, OBCs and SCs.Meanwhile, according to an official communication, Keralam governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar was shifted to Tamil Nadu, and Sikkim's Om Prakash Mathur will take charge in Keralam.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Conflict, drought increasing risk of famine in Sudan: Monitor
articles.summary: El Nino-induced drought is affecting roughly half of the country as three-year long war continues.
articles.body:
Conflict and drought are increasing the risk of famine across Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, warns a global food crisis monitor.

“An El Nino-induced drought, affecting roughly half of the country, is compounding the impacts of conflict and displacement, reducing food availability, driving up prices and affecting livelihoods,” the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said on Monday in a statement.

“Healthcare is extremely limited, often entirely inaccessible, while clean water is becoming increasingly scarce, leaving a poorly nourished population highly vulnerable to disease and death,” it added.

The IPC is an initiative aimed at enhancing food security and consists of 21 organisations and intergovernmental institutions, including the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the World Bank, the World Food Programme (WFP) and the World Health Organization (WHO).

‘Food insecurity, acute malnutrition and excess mortality’

Farmers’ livelihoods have deteriorated and dependence on food assistance is on the rise, said the IPC. “Food insecurity, acute malnutrition and excess mortality will likely intensify,” it warned.

Poor vegetation growth affects nearly two-thirds of cropland in North Darfur and about half in South Darfur, West Kordofan and South Kordofan, where severe water shortages and limited opportunity for agricultural recovery threaten livelihoods.

The IPC reported worsening acute malnutrition in additional areas, including Nyala, where the proportion of children accessing nutrition services who were admitted for severe acute malnutrition doubled from approximately 5% to 11% between January and August. Two displacement camps in South Darfur also recorded global acute malnutrition above famine thresholds.

In North Darfur, delayed rains that impacted crop cultivation and “critically low” food stocks have worsened food insecurity, it added. Western Kordofan is suffering one of its worst droughts since 2004 amid poor rainfall.

In May, nearly 19.5 million people, over 40% of the population, were facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to an IPC assessment. Of those, 135,000 were in Phase 5, the most severe classification, characterised by extreme food shortages, starvation, very high levels of malnutrition and deaths from disease or acute malnutrition.

Sudan’s war erupted in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), escalated into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, before spreading across the country. The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the actual toll is likely higher. About 13 million people have been displaced .

The army holds sway in Sudan’s central and eastern regions, while the Darfur region in the west and parts of the south are under control of the rival RSF.

The arid Darfur region, which is about the size of Spain, has faced some of the worst violence, with displacement camps invaded and ethnic cleansing killing thousands at a time.

articles.title: A London family kept a dirt-covered dish under a sofa for decades; rare Chinese imperial porcelain is estimated at £30,000
articles.summary: For decades, a large, dirt-covered porcelain dish lay beneath a sofa in a north London home, its significance unknown to the family who kept it.
articles.body: For decades, a large, dirt-covered porcelain dish lay beneath a sofa in a north London home, its significance unknown to the family who kept it. Now identified as a rare example of Chinese imperial porcelain associated with the court of Empress Dowager Cixi, the dish is expected to sell for £20,000 to £30,000 at auction. The 2ft-wide piece, which weighs about 30lb, was brought to Britain in the early 20th century by Chinese immigrant Wing Lung Goo and passed down through his family. Asian art specialist John Axford of Salisbury auction house Woolley & Wallis identified a four-character seal mark on its base linking it to Chuxiu Palace in Beijing’s Forbidden City. Decorated in imperial yellow with green and aubergine enamels, the dish is scheduled to be offered for sale on 10 November 2026. Asian art specialist John Axford identified the four-character seal mark on its base, which links the dish to Chuxiu Palace in Beijing’s Forbidden City. Comparable dishes bearing the same mark provide further context for understanding the piece and its place within late Qing imperial porcelain.Qing dynasty dish found under a sofa in Barnet: how the Goo family’s porcelain reached Woolley & WallisThe discovery began when a relative of the family contacted Woolley & Wallis and sent photographs of the dish. It had spent decades beneath the living-room sofa in a Barnet townhouse, where it accumulated dirt. Axford, the auction house’s Asian art specialist, decided that the object’s unusual size warranted an in-person inspection. Examining the dish revealed a seal mark on its underside that helped establish its significance. Axford said the family’s reason for storing the dish beneath the sofa was not known. He suggested that its size may have made it difficult to hang on a wall or display, although that explanation remains a possibility rather than an established account of the family’s decision. After it was cleaned, the porcelain emerged in what the auction house described as near-pristine condition.The discovery resembles other cases in which an ordinary-looking object has turned out to be more significant than its owners realised. In its article Charity Shop Finds, Woolley & Wallis recounts how a Chinese dish that was due to be priced at £2 in a Dorset charity shop was brought in for valuation and recognised by Axford. The Barnet dish, however, stands out for its monumental scale and its unusual base, which the auction house says is the only known example of this type to have a yellow glaze across the base as well.Chuxiugong zhi seal mark explained: how experts linked the dish to Empress Dowager CixiThe central clue is the four-character mark, Chuxiugong zhi, on the underside. It translates as “made for Chuxiu Palace”, also known as the Palace of Gathering Elegance. The palace was one of the six Western palaces in Beijing’s Forbidden City and was closely associated with Empress Dowager Cixi. According to Sotheby’s catalogue notes for a related yellow-ground dragon charger, Chuxiu Palace was Cixi’s chief residence between 1856 and 1885. She had it refurbished for her 50th birthday in 1884, with large decorative objects among the furnishings. Axford concluded that the Barnet dish was made in the 1880s to mark Cixi’s birthday. That dating places it in the late Qing dynasty, during the Guangxu period, which ran from 1875 to 1908. The seal is significant because it associates the object with a specific imperial palace rather than identifying it merely as Chinese porcelain. Its decoration provides further points of comparison with known palace wares.A related dish offered by Woolley & Wallis in 2023, documented in lot 40 of its Fine Asian Art sale, measures 32cm across. It features two scaly dragons contesting a flaming pearl amid clouds, with four dragons on the underside. Its recorded provenance includes Field Marshal Earl Kitchener and a 1938 Sotheby’s sale in London. Another comparison appears in Sotheby’s 2016 catalogue for a large yellow-ground dragon charger. That piece bears the same four-character mark and features two leaping dragons contesting a flaming pearl, with green and aubergine enamels against a yellow ground. Sotheby’s traces the design to a Kangxi-period prototype in the National Palace Museum in Taipei. These parallels help specialists place the Barnet dish within a recognisable tradition of imperial porcelain, although each object has its own features and history.Imperial Chinese porcelain at auction: what a £20,000 to £30,000 estimate says about the dishThe Barnet dish has several features that distinguish it from smaller examples. It measures about 61cm across and weighs approximately 30lb. Its decoration includes two confronting dragons contesting a flaming pearl, surrounded by clouds and flames. A floral border features lotus, prunus, peony, chrysanthemum and hibiscus, while further dragons and flaming pearls decorate the rim. The yellow ground, with green and aubergine enamel details, is characteristic of the group of imperial wares to which the dish has been linked. The base may be its most unusual feature. Woolley & Wallis has described the dish as the only known example of this type with a yellow-glazed base. The auction house says the combination of its scale, its association with Cixi’s court and the potentially unique base makes it a significant example of late Qing palace porcelain to appear on the market in recent years. The claim about the base is the auction house’s assessment of the known examples, rather than proof that no other example could exist.Previous auction results provide context for the estimate, although they are not direct price comparisons. The smaller 32cm Chuxiugong-marked dish offered by Woolley & Wallis in 2023 carried an estimate of £2,000 to £3,000 and sold for £8,820, including the buyer’s premium. Sotheby’s gave a large yellow-ground charger bearing the same mark an estimate of $60,000 to $80,000 in 2016. Its catalogue also records earlier sales of closely related dishes in Hong Kong and London. The Barnet dish is substantially larger than the 32cm example, and its yellow-glazed base is an additional point of distinction. Those characteristics help explain why the auction house has assigned it a higher estimate, although the final price will depend on bidding on the day. The dish is scheduled to be offered by Woolley & Wallis on 10 November 2026. For the Goo family, the object’s significance emerged only after a relative sought an expert opinion. Its journey from a family home to an auction catalogue illustrates how marks, decoration and comparisons with documented objects can change the understanding of a piece of porcelain that has remained in private hands for generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2020, Alex Trebek and Jean Trebek donated $500,000 to Hope of the Valley; two years later, the lead gift had helped turn a shuttered 60-year-old roller rink into the 23,000-square-foot, 107-bed Trebek Center
articles.summary: The legacy of late Jeopardy!
articles.body: The legacy of late Jeopardy! host Alex Trebek lives on through the Trebek Center, a 107-bed homeless shelter in Los Angeles that was developed with support from the television host and his wife, Jean. The facility, which was established at the site of the former Skateland roller rink, was created to provide people experiencing homelessness with accommodation and access to mental health services. Operated by Hope of the Valley Rescue Mission, the shelter was made possible through contributions from the Trebek family, private donors and the city of Los Angeles. The story of how it came to be was recounted by the organisation’s founder and CEO, Ken Craft, in a 2022 newsletter.How Alex Trebek first got involved with the homeless shelterIn the Easter 2022 edition of SharingHope, Hope of the Valley Rescue Mission founder and CEO Ken Craft recalled receiving an unexpected phone call from Trebek, who had heard about the organisation’s plans to build a homeless shelter and wanted to visit the site.Craft arranged a meeting, and the following morning, Trebek arrived wearing jeans and a baseball cap. After touring the proposed facility, the television host said he would be in touch.A few weeks later, Trebek called Craft to request the organisation’s audited financial statements. After reviewing them, he invited Craft to his home. Craft recalled finding the documents marked with highlights, circles and notes.Trebek told him that he appreciated the organisation’s social enterprises and the way it was being run. He then handed Craft a cheque for $100,000.Craft also recalled asking Trebek for a hug and a photograph. The host agreed to the hug and later arranged for Craft and his wife, Laurie, to visit the set of Jeopardy!. During the visit, Trebek brought them on stage and spoke about the homelessness crisis in Los Angeles and the mission’s work.The Trebek family’s $500,000 contributionCraft’s account also detailed a later visit by Trebek and his wife, Jean, to the organisation’s North Hollywood shelter. In June 2020, shortly before that shelter opened, Trebek contacted Craft to ask whether he could bring Jean to see a multipurpose room named in their honour.During the visit, Jean handed Craft a cheque for $500,000. The couple told him they believed in the organisation’s work and wanted to invest in its mission.Craft asked whether the contribution could serve as the lead donation for another shelter the organisation was planning to build. According to his account, the couple agreed.The donation helped initiate fundraising for the new facility. The organisation subsequently secured additional support from private donors and the city of Los Angeles to acquire the former Skateland property and convert it into accommodation for people experiencing homelessness.Why the shelter was named after Alex TrebekTrebek died in November 2020, before Craft could update him about the acquisition of the former roller rink property. Following his death, Craft contacted Jean to offer his condolences and ask whether the organisation could name the new shelter after her husband.In the newsletter, Craft recalled that Jean called him back the following day and said the family would be honoured to have Alex’s name on the building.The Trebek family later attended the groundbreaking ceremony, marking the beginning of the project.Jean also spoke about her husband’s commitment to the cause, saying, “I know how proud Alex was of their mission. He was so deeply grateful to be a part of the solution, to always lend a helping hand by offering both hope and practical assistance to those in need.”What the Trebek Center was designed to offerThe 107-bed facility was planned to provide people experiencing homelessness with a safe place to sleep, along with access to mental health services and other forms of support.The centre was developed as part of Hope of the Valley Rescue Mission’s broader efforts to address homelessness in Los Angeles. Its conversion from a former roller rink into a shelter reflected the organisation’s goal of creating accommodation while helping residents work towards greater stability.The organisation also invited supporters to sponsor bedrooms at the centre. Its 2022 newsletter outlined a $3,000 bedroom sponsorship programme, with contributions helping provide food, shelter and care for residents.The Trebek Center’s story is a reminder of how the late television host’s generosity extended beyond his career on Jeopardy!. Through his and Jean’s contributions, alongside support from other donors and the city, a former entertainment venue was transformed into a project intended to offer shelter and practical assistance to people in need.You use AI every day. articles.title: Endometriosis centres 'at risk' of closure as women's health 'broken'
articles.summary: Kelly O'Shea felt there was no alternative but to pay £20,000 for the treatment she needed out of desperation.
articles.body:
Kelly O'Shea says she has woken from more than one operation to be told adequate resources were not available to do the procedure she needed.

The 32-year-old, who lives with chronic pain, felt there was no alternative but to pay £20,000 for the endometriosis treatment she needed, out of frustration and desperation.

It comes as gynaecologists warn specialist centres in Wales dealing with complex cases of endometriosis are in jeopardy and a national service must be commissioned.

The deputy minister for women's health in Wales said the current set up was "not sustainable" and is discussing options for a regional or national service to be established.

Changes are being introduced by national accreditation body British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy (BSGE) highlighting the resource challenges faced by hospitals in Wales.

Clinical staff say it has been made worse because of the funding differences between England and Wales.

They say unless more resources are found to increase capacity and dedicate teams to endometriosis care, BSGE-accreditation requirements will not be met, which would lead to a downgrading of services, a potential skills exodus and large numbers of patients being sent to England for care.

At a recent cross-party Senedd group on women's health, gynaecologists said Wales either needed a nationally commissioned service or an overhaul of the funding model to better reflect the true cost of the specialist care.

The call is mirrored by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, who said the Welsh government must "commit to sustainable resourcing of gynaecology services - including adequate workforce numbers, staff training and appropriate facilities across the country".

Kelly said she had been in daily pain for about three and a half years, though her symptoms started when she was a teenager.

As mother to a young son, she said it affected everything. As her endometriosis is also in her bowel, she has been told she needs bowel and bladder specialists alongside endometriosis specialists during surgery.

After her last operation she said she was woken 45 minutes later to discover a bowel surgeon had been unavailable, so her endometriosis was left untouched. BBC Wales has spoken to another woman whose surgery was stopped in a different part of Wales, for the same reason.

On another occasion Kelly's surgery was cut short because the theatre was needed for an urgent case.

"I was promised we'd have the whole team there and they'd get me out of pain," she said.

"But it's always the same excuse - they weren't available, or they ran out of surgery time. You just think 'why are you putting me through an operation if you haven't got the surgery time?'

"Every time they go in I'm getting more and more scar tissue from these surgeries. As you can imagine, I've lost faith."

She said discussions were had about transferring her care to Bristol, but she was then told one of the other specialist centres in Wales would treat her.

The wait could be up to two years, she said, depending on clinical need.

"I've put so much on hold, I just want my life back," she said.

As a healthcare professional, Kelly said she had seen really good care in other parts of the NHS, yet felt "women's health is just completely broken".

Earlier this year Cardiff and Vale health board added their specialist endometriosis centre to their risk register, citing that changes by the BSGE could cause its closure unless changes were made to meet accreditation criteria.

Lutfi Shamsuddin, one of the team of endometriosis surgeons at the centre, told the cross-party meeting the issues centred around allocating dedicated time for a multi-disciplinary team to be involved in complex cases, and ensuring surgeons performed a minimum number of operations per year.

He said limited access to sufficient theatre time meant individual surgeons may be unable to carry out the volume of work required to meet the threshold for BSGE accreditation.

In addition, all accredited centres must have named gynaecologists, specialist nurses, colorectal surgeons, urologists and radiologists with time dedicated in their rota for endometriosis care at least six times a year.

However, he said his own centre relied on "the goodwill" of a radiologist or urologist when required, rather than having those roles planned into the endometriosis service.

It is estimated about one in 10 women have endometriosis. Shamsuddin said about 60% of patients can have their care managed by GPs in the community, however 40% are referred to hospital gynaecology teams.

For cases deemed to be "deep infiltrating endometriosis" which affects other organs such as the bladder and bowel, women in south Wales will be referred to one of two BSGE accredited centres. Cases in north Wales are sent to hospitals in Liverpool or Chester.

Cardiff and Vale also considers referrals from Cwm Taf Morgannwg, while Swansea Bay will receive referrals from Hywel Dda. Aneurin Bevan is understood to be seeking accreditation, and will consider referrals from Powys.

Gynaecologists told the meeting that the acute challenges in Cardiff "could easily be replicated by other centres in Wales".

Shamsuddin warned that losing accreditation would mean patients would be sent for care in England, at a higher cost to NHS Wales.

Abigail Holmes, clinical board director for women and children at the health board, told the meeting they were "working incredibly hard to make sure our service does not collapse".

She said "the only way the service can survive" was for it to be a nationally commissioned service by NHS Wales' joint commissioning committee (JCC).

The meeting heard representations have been made to the JCC by the gynaecology clinical improvement network, which is part of NHS performance and improvement, pressing the need for a pan-Wales approach.

Endometriosis services were discussed in June 2024 as a possible area to be commissioned by the JCC, however as no new investment was made available for 2026-27, national services were not established.

A spokesperson said it recognised the concern, but responsibility currently remains with individual health boards. It said it would continue to work with the Welsh government, health boards and others to support discussions.

The concerns about the future of the centre at Cardiff and Vale health board have prompted a petition, which has already reached more than 11,000 signatures.

David Fluck, executive medical director at the health board, said: "We recognise the importance of BSGE accreditation and are actively working towards reaccreditation when our current accredited period expires.

"We want to reassure patients that our endometriosis service is a core-funded health board service. We are working towards longer-term service sustainability and improvement in line with the women's health plan, with the needs of our patients at the heart of these discussions."

Swansea Bay University Health Board has not placed its service on a risk register, however it too has challenges around theatre capacity, workforce and sustainable multidisciplinary support for complex surgery.

Delyth Jewell MS, deputy minister for women's health, said she had been assured by the chair of Cardiff and Vale health board, Kirsty Williams, that it was taking the necessary steps to maintain accreditation.

"Everyone agrees the current set up is not sustainable," she said.

"We can't be leaving this to the goodwill of individual health boards. I'm keen for us to be looking regionally or nationally, to make sure there is a sustainable service.

"Because women already wait too long to have endometriosis symptoms spotted. It's non-negotiable for me - we have to make sure these services continue to be made available."

articles.title: Lockerbie bombing suspect seized from Libya in 'cloak and dagger' operation
articles.summary: Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi claims he was unlawfully taken from Libya to stand trial over the bombing.
articles.body:
A Lockerbie bombing suspect has claimed he was illegally removed from Libya to stand trial in the United States after "a cloak and dagger operation conducted in the dead of night".

Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has alleged he was abducted by armed men and handed over "hooded and bound" to FBI agents, who had a plane waiting to fly him out of the country.

Al-Marimi, also known as Mas'ud, has denied building and priming the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie on 21 December 1988, killing 270 people.

The Libyan argues he was the victim of an unlawful rendition and has asked a judge in Washington DC to throw the case out of court.

In response, the US Department of Justice said, under American law, the manner of his removal should not stop his thrice-postponed trial from finally getting underway in January.

Al-Marimi's version of what happened is detailed for the first time in papers lodged with the court by his legal team.

Lockerbie bombing trial date set as judge warns against further delay

I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questions

The US government charged him with destroying the airliner in December 2020, and formally requested his "extradition, expulsion or otherwise lawful removal" from Libya to stand trial.

At the time, Al-Marimi was in custody in Libya, serving a jail sentence for attacking rebel forces during the uprising against Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

According to Al-Marimi, he was released from prison on "compassionate grounds" on 30 September 2021 and returned to his family in Tripoli.

About two weeks later, a group of armed men, many wearing masks, came to his house and rearrested him, without telling him why or who they were.

Defence lawyers claim his "abduction" was reportedly carried out by a militia with "a reputation for brutality and disdain for human rights".

They allege Al-Marimi was dragged across the floor "with no care for his health and mobility issues", that his son was beaten with a rifle, and that his wife and daughter were attacked.

They said the grandfather was taken to a prison in the city of Misrata, about 116 miles (187km) east of Tripoli, where he was placed in solitary confinement for several days.

On the morning of 11 December 2022, Al-Marimi said his captors gave him a sandwich and some tea and told him to pack his belongings.

He expected to be released, but instead he was handed over to the FBI.

A US government aircraft was waiting at Misrata airport when Al-Marimi arrived with a "loosely fitted cloth hood" over his head.

His escorts asked the FBI to hurry up because onlookers were watching and he was placed on board the plane.

The Libyan authorities handed over a plastic "trash bag" containing some of his belongings, including a Quran, a prayer rug, clothing, toiletries, and medicine.

On the flight to the US, the FBI questioned Al-Marimi, performed a "head to toe medical examination" and provided him with clean clothes and blankets, his lawyers said.

They claim the prime minister of the Tripoli-based Libyan government, Abdulhamid Dbeibah, later secured financial investment from the United States, including $16m (£12m) to secure Libya's transition to a democratic state and a contract with US oil giant Honeywell International.

Al-Marimi argues that the process amounted to an unlawful rendition and forcible abduction, removing the Washington court's jurisdiction over the case.

The defence says the militia group staged an illegal kidnapping when diplomatic negotiations stalled, in a process which showed "an utter disregard for Libyan law and sovereignty."

His lawyers said: "This is not the rule of law.

"This is the rule of the strong. Mr Al-Marimi's rendition sends a chilling message to the people of the world: 'If we want you, we will take you'."

They added: "Mr Al-Marimi must be returned to Libya."

The US Government said that, under longstanding legal doctrine, the court's jurisdiction was not contingent on the manner by which the defendant had been brought before it, even if that included forcible abduction.

The prosecutors said limited exceptions to that rule did not apply in Al-Marimi's case.

In their submission to the court, the government said: "Libya was permitted to transfer the defendant to the United States under any method it chose."

They added: "Any actions of the Libyan militias are not attributable to the United States, as would be required for this claim to succeed."

The defence has asked for a hearing so it can argue its case before Judge Dabney Friedrich.

Al-Marimi's removal from Libya in 2022 provoked a fierce backlash in his home country.

Prime Minister Debeibah said his government had been co-operating with an "international judicial framework to extradite accused citizens."

An Interpol red notice was in force at the time, requesting law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest Al-Marimi, pending his extradition or surrender.

The head of Scotland's prosecution service, the-then Lord Advocate Dorothy Bain KC, told the Scottish Parliament she had received confirmation that Al-Marimi was transferred to US custody "on a lawful basis".
